title: Antibiotic Prophylaxis in Surgical Patients: A Retrospective Analysis at a Secondary Hospital in Trinidad and Tobago
content: Background: Antibiotic prophylaxis is a critical intervention in reducing postoperative infections, yet inappropriate prescribing remains a global contributor to antimicrobial resistance (AMR). Trinidad and Tobago lacks localized data on perioperative antibiotic practices, hindering effective antimicrobial stewardship. The aim of this paper was to assess the prescribing patterns, appropriateness, and outcomes of prophylactic antibiotic use across various surgical departments at the Sangre Grande Hospital, a secondary care hospital in eastern Trinidad. Methods: A retrospective observational study was conducted on 235 randomly selected patient records from January 2024 to April 2025. Data included demographics, surgical category, type and route of antibiotics administered, duration of hospital stay, and use of microbiological testing. Antibiotics were classified using the WHO AWaRe framework. Results: Among the 235 patients, n=124 52.8% were female and n=111, 47.2% were male. General surgery accounted for the majority of procedures n=175 (74.5%). Antibiotic prophylaxis was administered in n= 225, 85.1% of cases. The majority n=140, 62.2% were from the WHO “Access” category and n=85, 37.8% from the “Watch” category. Augmentin n=100 (44.4%), Ceftriaxone n=57 (25.3%), and Metronidazole n=39 (17.3%) were the most frequently used antibiotics. Most antibiotics were delivered intravenously 155 (66%). Only four patients (1.7%) had microbiological cultures sent, despite the availability of susceptibility testing. The surgical site infection (SSI) rate was low (0.44%), and n=102, 45.5% of patients were discharged within one day post-surgery. Conclusion: This study reveals widespread empirical antibiotic use with low reliance on culture-based prescribing. Despite a low SSI rate, the underutilization of microbiological testing and the reliance on “Watch” category antibiotics present stewardship concerns. This article bridges antibiotic stewardship with infection prevention and control and emphasizes the utility of combining the two disciplines.
